source.title: On Statistical Properties of Sharpness-Aware Minimization: Provable Guarantees

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper studies SAM versus GD prediction error and sharpness, but none of the listed versions tests SAM, and its sharpness measure is not the magnitude-aware measure specified in V7.
record.gate_note: The paper reports SAM/GD validation accuracy and theoretical prediction-error comparisons. These do not test the listed versions: the optimizer comparison is not adaptive methods versus SGD (V4), and the sharpness analysis does not measure magnitude-aware sharpness tracking the train-test gap (V7). The paper also reports numerical comparisons of ρ values; these are not rows because ρ is not a versioned intervention.
record.test_reason: Appendix F.3.4 and Table F.2 compare batch sizes 256 and 512 at fixed epoch budgets using sample-split SAM on ResNet50. These results bear on V5 in a new training setting. The main SAM-versus-SGD comparisons and the unscaled theoretical sharpness measure do not test the other versions.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is broadly accurate. The authors establish conditional prediction-error advantages for SAM in fixed-activation hidden-layer ReLU networks and indefinite kernel regression, alongside conditional flatness results. Their experiments generally agree with these insights, and they conclude that sample splitting does not help relative to optimal unsplit SAM.
record.recipe_differences: The study analyzes and evaluates Sharpness-Aware Minimization (SAM) against gradient descent (GD); it does not apply the original studies' interventions or measurements represented by the claim versions.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported outcomes vary with dataset label noise, training epoch, and SAM ρ; larger ρ helps earlier in training, while its gains can fade later.

fits_no_version.finding: SAM and SAM-Decay often improve CIFAR validation accuracy over momentum SGD, with outcomes depending on label noise, training duration, and perturbation radius.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAM can improve validation performance over momentum SGD in these ResNet CIFAR settings.

fits_no_version.finding: Under stated assumptions, SAM has lower prediction error than GD and can have lower unscaled local loss sharpness. Convex noisy settings involve a bias-variance tradeoff; indefinite kernels can yield bounded SAM error while GD error diverges.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Conditional theoretical prediction-error advantages of SAM can coincide with lower unscaled sharpness.

record.problems: Deep-network results are limited to CIFAR10/100 with ResNet18/50; experiments are reported with three repetitions in Appendix F.3.1. The study does not test memorization of random labels, and its sharpness result is theoretical rather than a measured magnitude-aware sharpness-to-gap ranking.
record.rows_left_out: No additional eligible results omitted. The paper's theoretical SAM/GD prediction-error comparisons concern linearized one-hidden-layer ReLU networks and kernel regression, not the listed versions; figures for theoretical curves are discussed as illustrations rather than measurements of any listed version.

untested.parts: Near-perfect fitting of fixed random labels alongside natural-label generalization and chance-level random-label held-out accuracy.
Test error as width increases beyond the width needed for zero training error.
Convolutional versus fully connected architectures and the role of learned local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD under limited or broader tuning.

The workload-dependent batch-size threshold, behavior beyond 512, standard unsplit training across batch sizes, language models, and the specified learning-rate, warmup, normalization, and regularization remedies.
Dropout interventions and interactions with training-set size, augmentation, or weight decay.
Magnitude-scaled perturbation tolerance, measured train-test gaps among similarly fitted convolutional networks, and comparison with norm- and margin-based rankings.
Removing highly memorized examples versus equally many random examples and retraining.

missing.what: CIFAR10, 200 epochs: sample-split SAM validation accuracy is 94.39 ± 0.11 at batch 256 and 95.03 ± 0.09 at batch 512. Add a batch-size comparison row.
CIFAR10, 400 epochs: sample-split SAM validation accuracy is 94.73 ± 0.11 at batch 256 and 95.50 ± 0.04 at batch 512. Add a batch-size comparison row.

CIFAR100, 200 epochs: sample-split SAM validation accuracy is 78.63 ± 0.48 at batch 256 and 78.72 ± 0.42 at batch 512. Add a batch-size comparison row; the reported difference is small relative to variability.

CIFAR100, 400 epochs: sample-split SAM validation accuracy is 78.95 ± 0.30 at batch 256 and 79.55 ± 0.33 at batch 512. Add a batch-size comparison row. For all four comparisons, each batch is divided equally between the ascent and descent gradients.

record.verdict_notes: The study is not an original source for V5. Its batch-size evidence was overlooked by the record. The sample-splitting-versus-unsplit-SAM comparison itself does not isolate batch size; the within-Table-F.2 comparisons do.

versions.untested_parts: Memorization of random labels and generalization on natural labels.
Width sweeps beyond the interpolation threshold.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD or momentum SGD.
Large versus small batches under fixed epoch budgets.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and its ranking against other gap measures.
Removal of memorized examples and its effect on test accuracy.

conditions.value: SAM ρ not stated in this passage; GD ρ=0

rows.measure: Classification accuracy on the validation set over epochs.
rows.value: SAM has better accuracy over GD for almost all epochs.
rows.note: The reported measure is validation accuracy, not training error or a train-test gap; the passage gives no precise values.
rows.check: No listed version measures SAM versus SGD validation accuracy alone. The deep-learning baseline called GD uses minibatches and momentum 0.9, with weight decay 0.0005 (Appendix F.3.1).

rows.subject: ResNet50
rows.operation_detail: Compared SAM and GD validation accuracy over epochs on noisy CIFAR10 labels.
rows.measure: Validation classification accuracy over epochs; the text says both methods overfit later in training and the performance gap grows under noise.
rows.value: SAM performs better than GD in the noisy setup, with a larger gap described as noise increases.
rows.note: The text does not assign precise Figure 2 values to the individual random and worse conditions in this passage. The measure does not establish any listed version.
rows.check: The random and worse conditions contain approximately 17% and 40% noisy human annotations; they are not fully randomized labels as in V1. Neither training-label memorization nor chance-level held-out accuracy is measured. The baseline is minibatch momentum SGD.

relationships.condition: ResNet50 with sample-split SAM on CIFAR10 and CIFAR100; batch size 256 versus 512 at fixed budgets of 200 or 400 epochs.
relationships.reason: Table F.2, absent from the rows, reports higher validation accuracy with batch 512 in all four comparisons. Larger batches therefore do not incur a penalty over this tested range; the experiment does not establish whether either size exceeds the workload-dependent threshold.
relationships.display_finding: Higher validation accuracy with the larger batch was reported in all four comparisons, but these comparisons remain unverified. They do not identify a batch size above which accuracy falls.
